questions.prompt: On a POSIX system, what does this program print?
questions.explanation: `operator/` follows the rules of `append`: if the right-hand operand is absolute, it replaces the left-hand path instead of being joined to it. The result is `/opt`. Plain string concatenation would give the first option, which is what `+=` on a path does for relative text.

The extension is the part of the filename from the last dot, so it is `.gz`, and the stem is everything before that, which is `archive.tar`. Peeling several extensions requires calling `stem()` repeatedly.

questions.prompt: On a POSIX system, what does this program print?
questions.explanation: `exists` and `is_regular_file` use `status`, which follows symlinks, so a symlink whose target is missing is reported as not existing. `is_symlink` uses `symlink_status`, which looks at the link itself, and finds one. To ask about the link, use the `symlink_status` family.

Normalization removes `b/..` and then `a/..`, leaving nothing. The standard says that if the result would be empty it is a single dot. An empty path means no path at all, so the dot is the way to name the current directory.

questions.prompt: On a POSIX system, what does this program print?
questions.explanation: The operating system resolves `link/..` by following the link first, so it names the parent of `real/sub`, which is `real`. Lexical normalization knows nothing about links and cancels `link/..`, leaving `root`, which is a different directory. That is why `lexically_normal` is unsafe on paths that may contain symlinks, and why `canonical` exists.

Path comparison goes element by element, and repeated separators do not create extra elements, so `a//b` equals `a/b`. A trailing separator does produce a final empty element, and `.` is an element, so the other two comparisons are false. Comparison never normalizes.

No: a `path` cannot be constructed from a `u8` literal
questions.explanation: C++20 changed `path::u8string()` to return `std::u8string`, because UTF-8 text now has its own character type. A `std::u8string` cannot be converted to `std::string`. In C++17, where `u8` literals are `char`, the same code compiles. Construction from a `u8` literal is fine in both versions.

The overload taking an `error_code&` reports failure through the argument and never throws a `filesystem_error`; the standard specifies that `file_size` returns `static_cast<uintmax_t>(-1)` on error. Without the `ec` argument, the same call throws. The `ec` argument is set to the system's error code.
